en.title: About — Norayr Avetisyan
en.description: Senior Fullstack Engineer in Yerevan, writing JavaScript and TypeScript since 2018. Experience, stack, and the questions a hiring manager asks.

lead.text: I build interfaces that many people use, and the systems they run on.

paragraphs.text: I've written JavaScript and TypeScript since 2018. At MTS Web Services I built a design system of 200+ components used by 15+ teams across a 10M+ MAU ecosystem. At Vizogen I took a multi-tenant AI SaaS module's LCP from 4.1s to 1.3s, and designed its schemas, row-level security and REST contracts.

In 2025 I founded Proof App and built it alone: the Telegram Mini App, a Postgres backend of 40+ tables with row-level security, 16 Edge Functions and the job queues behind them. It reached a closed beta. Now I work on two web apps at Fendr, from the monorepo up.
I'm looking for a senior fullstack role at a remote EU or US product company, where the interface and the system under it are the same job.

content.name: Norayr Avetisyan

items.a: In products: at Proof App one Gemini 2.5 Flash pass judges reps, form and liveness. At Vizogen I rolled out team-wide AI-assisted workflows with Cursor and custom MCP servers. In my own work I use Claude Code and Cursor, and I review what they write before it ships.

en.title: FilterGraph — faceted search demo
en.description: A demo: faceted search that keeps its filters in the address, so any view is a link you can send.

content.title: FilterGraph
content.description: Faceted search over a sample catalogue. Filters depend on each other, and the address bar holds them, so any view is a link you can send.

decisions.body: Every filter is written to the query string and read back from it on load, so refresh and a shared link both land on the same view.
decisions.title: The address is the state.

decisions.body: Choosing a category narrows what the other filters offer.
decisions.title: Facets know their dependencies.

decisions.body: The product modal walks through a three-step order with test fields. Nothing is charged or sent.
decisions.title: Checkout is a mock.

en.title: MerchForge — merch configurator demo
en.description: A demo: a merch configurator where the preview, the price and the JSON are all read from one configuration.

content.title: MerchForge
content.description: A merch configurator. Every control writes to one configuration, and the preview, the price and the JSON output are all read from it.

decisions.body: Product, colour, size, text and quantity live in one object. Nothing else stores a copy.
decisions.title: One source of truth.

decisions.body: The price and the output are computed from that object on every change, so they can't disagree with the preview.
decisions.title: Derived, not stored.

decisions.body: The JSON panel animates the new text in, so you can see what each change did.
decisions.title: The output types itself out.

en.title: NexusRoute — logistics map demo
en.description: A demo: a Leaflet map with simulated shipments between 12 hub cities, and a stress test you can run in the browser.

content.title: NexusRoute
content.description: A logistics map on Leaflet: simulated shipments and routes between 12 hub cities, drawn from GeoJSON. The stress test adds 40 markers, ten per animation frame.

decisions.body: The stress test adds ten markers per animation frame, so the map paints between batches instead of freezing until the last one.
decisions.title: Markers arrive in batches.

decisions.body: Leaflet is its own chunk, fetched when this page opens, so no other page pays for it.
decisions.title: The map loads when it's needed.

decisions.body: Hubs, markers and routes are plain feature collections, the format a real tracking feed would send.
decisions.title: The data is GeoJSON.

en.title: OmniGrid — data grid demo
en.description: A demo: 100 sample shipments in a headless TanStack Table, cached by TanStack Query and checked by Zod.

content.title: OmniGrid
content.description: A data grid over 100 sample shipments. TanStack Table renders it without owning its markup, TanStack Query caches it, and Zod checks every response.

decisions.body: TanStack Table owns sorting and filtering; the markup is mine, so the grid looks like the rest of the page.
decisions.title: Headless table.

decisions.body: TanStack Query serves the rows it has at once and refetches in the background after 30 seconds. The panel beside the grid shows the cache's state.
decisions.title: Cached, then fresh.

decisions.body: Every response is parsed with Zod before the grid sees it, so a wrong shape fails in one place.
decisions.title: Checked at the boundary.

en.title: norav.dev — the site and the CMS behind it
en.description: How this site works: a CMS on Next.js and raw PostgreSQL, a snapshot baked into every build, and what it costs to run it alone.

content.retro: Was it worth it? As a content tool, no: a hosted CMS would have cost far less time for a site that changes once a month. As evidence of how I work, yes: I can open any layer of it in an interview, from a migration to the first paint. I'd wire the site rebuild into the release script on day one, and publish early. The September rebuild merged 21 PRs, and none of its copy went live for six weeks.
content.title: norav.dev
content.context: norav.dev is my portfolio, and the CMS behind it is part of the portfolio. The site is Vite and React 19, prerendered at build time. The CMS is Next.js on raw PostgreSQL, with no ORM. The two share one package of block schemas. I wanted the site to show how I work, not just list it, and a CMS I can open in an interview does that. I built both, and I run both, alone.

figures.alt: The CMS editor open on this case study. Above the form, "Validation failed" names one field, translations.en.decisions.3.body, as too short.
figures.caption: The CMS, running locally, refusing to save this page: a decision with no reasoning, and the field it's in.

metrics.label: automated tests: site, CMS and schema

content.outcome: On the mobile preset, the home page scores 100 in all four Lighthouse categories, with LCP at 1.3 seconds. Owning it has a cost, and it's real. In early November 2026, production was 14 migrations behind main, and the September rebuild's copy had never gone live. A 4.5 MB request limit on Vercel had quietly broken larger uploads. Now every release runs one rehearsed sequence: backup, rehearsal on a copy, dry run, then the change.
content.problem: A portfolio has to be fast and must never break. A CMS adds a database, an admin and a deploy, and each of them can fail. The site has to paint without waiting for the CMS. And a publish must not be able to ship a page that renders broken.

decisions.body: Each build bakes the published snapshot into the bundle, and every route is prerendered to HTML. The first paint makes no request to the CMS, and a CMS outage can't break a deploy. Once the page is idle, it asks the CMS for a checksum and swaps in newer content only if it differs. The cost: two copies of the content, and a publish reaches the first paint only after a rebuild.
decisions.title: Bake the content into the build, then revalidate

decisions.body: Each of the 28 block types is a Zod schema in a shared package. The admin draws its forms from it, publish validates every block against it, and the site takes its types from it. A page that would render broken can't be published. The cost: validation checks shape, not truth, so a false claim passes. And removing a block type takes two releases: retire its rows, then its code.
decisions.title: One block registry for the admin, publish and the site

decisions.body: There are 35 numbered SQL migrations, never edited once shipped. The schema tests apply them all to PGlite, Postgres compiled to WebAssembly, and local development runs on it with no database server. Each publication is an immutable row, so any version can be read back. The cost: no ORM writes a migration for me, and content changes are SQL written by hand.
decisions.title: Raw SQL and append-only migrations, tested on an embedded Postgres

content.description: This site, and the CMS I wrote to run it. Next.js and raw PostgreSQL on one side, Vite and React 19 on the other, joined by a snapshot that's baked into every build and revalidated after the page loads.

en.title: Nova Prism — a trading platform in four apps
en.description: A contract-first Fastify and Socket.IO API, a trading engine with stop-out and liquidation, and three front ends in one monorepo, with 58 test files.

content.retro: I'd split the engine from the API before adding anything else. Today the price feed, the engine, the sockets and the REST API share one Node process and one SQLite file. That kept it simple to build and to test. It's also the first thing to move if it ever needs a second machine.
content.title: Nova Prism
content.context: Nova Prism is a trading platform in one pnpm monorepo. A landing site shows live prices. In the client portal, people watch markets, open leveraged positions, set alerts and talk to support. In the host panel, the operator manages clients, balances and live positions. Under all three is one API on Node 24: REST, WebSocket, a trading engine and price feeds.

figures.alt: Nova Prism's landing page: the headline "Five markets. One account." beside a panel of five prices, over a scrolling ticker.
figures.caption: The landing site. A local run, with simulated prices.

figures.alt: The client portal's trading screen: a BTC/USD candle chart, the account's margin figures across the top, and an order form at 10x leverage showing the margin it needs.
figures.caption: The trading screen, on a seeded sample account.

figures.alt: The portfolio over ten seconds: equity, floating P/L, margin level and the P/L of two open positions change as each price tick arrives.
figures.caption: Ten seconds of ticks. Equity, P/L and margin level move with every one.

metrics.label: REST operations, each called in tests

content.outcome: The four apps start with one command on a seeded local database, and ship as two Docker images behind Caddy. The API tests boot the real Fastify app on an in-memory database and replay recorded Binance data. Playwright runs the portal and the landing site at three widths, in light and dark, with axe, and fails on a console error or a sideways scroll.
content.problem: A trading screen is only as good as its numbers. Price, P/L, margin level and stop-out have to agree in the engine, the portal and the host panel, while prices move every second. Four apps on one API also drift apart fast: a renamed field becomes a blank column somewhere else.

decisions.body: One OpenAPI file describes all 70 REST operations, and one typed file describes all 25 Socket.IO events. The API registers its routes from the contract and refuses one that isn't in it. Outside production, it checks every response against it. A test fails unless every operation is registered and has been called successfully. The cost: every endpoint starts as YAML, and production skips the response check.
decisions.title: The contract comes first, and a test enforces it

decisions.body: Margin, P/L and liquidation math live in one package. The engine settles trades with it, and the client portal draws its numbers with the same code. Money is a decimal string from the database to the screen, never a float. The cost: decimal.js in the portal's bundle, and a change to the math changes every app at once.
decisions.title: One copy of the trading math, in decimals

decisions.body: Open positions are held in memory. Each price tick checks stop-loss, take-profit and margin for the positions on that symbol. Below the stop-out level, the engine closes the worst-losing position, then checks again. SQLite through better-sqlite3 is synchronous, so a settlement can't interleave with an order. The cost: one API process and one database file. Scaling out means moving the engine out first.
decisions.title: Settle every tick in one process

content.description: A trading platform in four apps: a landing site with live prices, a client portal for leveraged trading, a host panel, and the API under them. Fastify and Socket.IO, a trading engine, contracts checked against OpenAPI, and 58 test files.

en.title: Proof App — a Telegram fitness app I built alone
en.description: A Telegram Mini App where one Gemini 2.5 Flash call counts reps and checks form and liveness. Built alone and taken to a closed beta.

content.title: Proof App
content.description: A Telegram fitness app I built as the only engineer and took to a closed beta. One Gemini 2.5 Flash pass judges reps, form and liveness. Under it: 40+ Postgres tables with row-level security, 70+ migrations, 16 Edge Functions and 3 pgmq job queues.

content.retro: I'd test the database first. The rules that matter most, points, energy and payments, are SQL, and nothing checked them but people using the app. I'd start with the queue and an event-driven worker, instead of meeting the timeout and the quota one at a time. And I'd keep to the core loop until it had real users: seasonal events and a paywall A/B test went in first.
content.context: Proof App is a fitness game inside Telegram. You film a set of squats or push-ups, a model judges it, and you earn points, a streak and a level. I built it alone, from November 2025 to June 2026: the Mini App, the Postgres backend, 16 Edge Functions, and payments in Telegram Stars. It reached a closed beta and went no further. It has no automated tests.
content.outcome: In the closed beta the loop worked end to end: film a set, get a verdict, earn points, and buy Premium with Telegram Stars. Each video is deleted as soon as it's judged. Then, in June 2026, the free tier ran out. Two cron jobs polled the workers every 10 seconds, about 518,000 calls a month, and Supabase began refusing every function, sign-in included. Now the trigger that queues a job calls the worker directly, and polling is a five-minute safety net.
content.problem: The game is only worth playing if the check is honest. One Gemini 2.5 Flash call does it. It asks for a random gesture at the start, so the clip is live and not a replay, then counts only the reps with acceptable form. That call could take up to 90 seconds. It runs from a webview on a phone network, and every rule about points has to hold when the phone can't be trusted.

decisions.body: At first the request waited for Gemini, up to 90 seconds, and Supabase cut it off with HTTP 546. Now the phone inserts a pending row. A trigger puts a job on a pgmq queue, a worker calls Gemini, and the verdict comes back over Realtime, with polling if that drops. The cost is a queue, a worker and retries to run. A failed job now marks the proof failed with a reason, because a silent retry looked like an endless spinner.
decisions.title: Judge the video on a queue, not in the request

decisions.body: Points are computed in the worker, never on the phone. Energy, streaks, referral gates and subscription renewals are triggers and functions, and 41 of 42 tables have row-level security. The phone can't award itself points or set its own price. The cost: that logic sits in 73 SQL migrations with no tests. When a platform grant changed, a trigger running as the caller made every proof upload fail.
decisions.title: Put the rules in Postgres, not in the app

decisions.body: Phones film large files, and the model needs far less. FFmpeg.wasm turns each clip into 480p at one frame a second, with no audio, aiming under 1 MB. It runs single-threaded: threads need cross-origin isolation, which I left out so the app kept working inside Telegram. So compression is slower, and Gemini judges one frame a second. If compression fails, the original uploads.
decisions.title: Compress on the phone, before the upload
